title: The Japanese Covered Bridge – Lai Vien Kieu
summary: A covered wooden bridge and the symbol of Hoi An, linked to the Japanese merchant community of the 17th century.
content:
Hello, and welcome to the Japanese Covered Bridge, known locally as Chua Cau, the most famous symbol of Hoi An Ancient Town. You are standing in front of a small roofed wooden bridge, about eighteen metres long, spanning a creek that flows into the Hoai River.

According to historical records and local legend, the bridge was built by Japanese merchants around the late sixteenth or early seventeenth century. At that time, Hoi An, which Western traders called Faifo, was a thriving international port. Merchant ships from Japan, China, Portugal and the Netherlands anchored here to trade silk, porcelain, agarwood and many other precious goods. The bridge connected the Japanese quarter on the west side with the Chinese quarter on the east.

In 1719, Lord Nguyen Phuc Chu visited Hoi An and gave the bridge the name Lai Vien Kieu, meaning the bridge for welcoming friends from afar. The wooden plaque bearing these three Chinese characters still hangs above the walkway today. So why do locals call it Chua Cau, the Bridge Pagoda? Because a small temple was later added on its northern side, dedicated to Bac De Tran Vo, the Emperor of the North, a deity believed to protect the land from floods and natural disasters. A bridge with a temple, a temple on a bridge, and so the name Chua Cau became familiar over many generations.

A fascinating legend tells of a gigantic sea monster whose head lay in India, its tail in Japan and its back beneath Hoi An. Whenever it stirred, it caused earthquakes and floods. The bridge was built like a sword, pinning the monster down and keeping this land peaceful.

Now look at the two ends of the bridge. On one side stand a pair of wooden monkeys, and on the other a pair of wooden dogs. There are several explanations, the most popular being that construction began in a Year of the Monkey and was completed in a Year of the Dog. Others believe these animals were sacred in Japanese beliefs.

Over more than four centuries, the bridge has been restored many times, so its present architecture blends Japanese, Chinese and Vietnamese influences. The most recent major restoration was completed in 2024, reinforcing the foundations, the wooden frame and the tiled roof to preserve the monument for future generations.

As you cross the bridge, take your time. Listen to the water flowing below and imagine the merchants of centuries past walking across these same boards. Please keep the area clean and do not touch the sacred statues. We wish you truly memorable moments here, at the very heart of Hoi An Ancient Town.

title: Phung Hung Old House
summary: A merchant family's wooden house over two hundred years old, blending Vietnamese, Japanese and Chinese architecture.
content:
Welcome to Phung Hung Old House, one of the oldest and most beautiful old houses in Hoi An, located just a short walk from the Japanese Covered Bridge. The house was built around the end of the eighteenth century, making it more than two hundred years old, and it has been home to many generations of the same family.

The name Phung Hung means prosperity and flourishing. In the past, this was the shop of a merchant family who traded in goods such as cinnamon, pepper, salt, silk, porcelain and glassware. The front of the house was used for business and receiving guests, while the back was the family's living quarters.

What makes Phung Hung Old House so special is the meeting of three architectural styles. You can recognise a Japanese-style roof on the upper floor, a gallery and balustrade in the Chinese style, while the overall layout and the arrangement of space are distinctly Vietnamese. This harmonious combination reflects the history of Hoi An itself, a place where different communities lived and traded side by side.

Please look up at the columns. The house is supported by about eighty columns made of ironwood, a precious, extremely hard and durable timber. Each column rests on a stone base. This technique keeps the wood from touching the damp ground, protecting it from termites and rot, which is why the house has been able to stand firm through hundreds of rainy seasons.

Speaking of floods, they are an inseparable part of life in Hoi An. Every year, around October and November, the Hoai River can rise and spill into the streets. That is why the upper floor of this house has trapdoors. When the water rises, the family uses pulleys to haul goods and furniture up through these openings to keep them safe on the upper level. It is a very clever solution devised by people of the past.

When you go upstairs, you will see the ancestral altar placed high and suspended. For Vietnamese people, worshipping grandparents and ancestors is extremely important, and the altar is always placed in the most respected position in the home.

Today, the family still looks after the house and showcases traditional hand embroidery. This is a chance to feel that an old house is not only a heritage site, but also a living home. During your visit, please walk softly, speak quietly and respect the family's private space. Thank you, and enjoy your visit.

title: Cantonese Assembly Hall
summary: The meeting place of the Chinese community from Guangdong, dedicated to Guan Yu and famous for its porcelain mosaic dragon.
content:
Welcome to the Cantonese Assembly Hall, also known as the Quang Trieu Assembly Hall. This was the gathering place of Chinese merchants from Guangzhou and Zhaoqing, two areas of Guangdong Province in China. The hall was built in the late nineteenth century, around 1885 according to many records.

So what exactly is an assembly hall? When Chinese people came to Hoi An to trade and settle, they usually founded assembly halls according to their home regions. An assembly hall served both as a place to worship deities and as a place to meet, support one another, handle common affairs and preserve the customs of their homeland. Hoi An has five major Chinese assembly halls, those of Fujian, Guangdong, Chaozhou, Hainan and the Chinese community as a whole, and each has its own character.

The Cantonese Assembly Hall is dedicated to Guan Yu, also called Quan Cong, a famous general of the Three Kingdoms period. Guan Yu is revered as a symbol of loyalty, righteousness and trustworthiness. For merchants, trust was the most valuable thing in business, which is why his image holds the place of honour in the main hall.

As you pass through the gate, notice the structure of the building. Many of the stone and wooden components are said to have been carved in advance in Guangdong and then shipped to Hoi An for assembly. The stone columns and the delicate wood carvings of flowers, birds, animals and scenes from ancient tales display the remarkable skill of the craftsmen of old.

Perhaps the most popular spot for visitors is the garden at the back. Here you will find a large dragon made from colourful pieces of broken porcelain, winding beside a small pond. This porcelain mosaic technique is very common in southern Chinese architecture, being both beautiful and resistant to sun and rain. Nearby there is also a carp, recalling the legend of the carp that leaps over the Dragon Gate and turns into a dragon, a symbol of perseverance and success.

After several restorations, the Cantonese Assembly Hall still retains both its solemn and lively atmosphere. The Chinese community of Hoi An still holds traditional festivals here, especially the Lantern Festival on the fifteenth day of the first lunar month, when the hall is brightly decorated with lanterns and fragrant incense.

The Cantonese Assembly Hall is vivid evidence of the cultural exchange between the Vietnamese and Chinese communities in the port town of Hoi An. During your visit, please keep quiet and do not touch the statues or ritual objects. We hope you enjoy the experience.

title: Museum of Sa Huynh Culture
summary: A museum preserving artefacts of the Iron Age Sa Huynh culture, dating back more than two thousand years.
content:
Welcome to the Museum of Sa Huynh Culture. If the Japanese Covered Bridge and the old houses tell you the story of Hoi An a few hundred years ago, this museum will take you much further back in time, to the people who lived on this land more than two thousand years ago.

Sa Huynh culture was an Iron Age culture that flourished along the central coast of Vietnam from around the late first millennium before the Common Era to the first centuries of the Common Era. Its name comes from Sa Huynh in Quang Ngai Province, where archaeologists discovered the first sites of this culture in 1909. Many other sites were found later, including several in the Hoi An area itself, such as Hau Xa and Thanh Chiem.

The most distinctive feature of Sa Huynh culture is jar burial. The Sa Huynh people buried their dead in large covered pottery jars, together with many grave goods such as pots, bowls, working tools, weapons and jewellery. In the museum, you can admire these burial jars, which help us imagine the spiritual beliefs and daily life of these ancient people.

Please take some time to look at the jewellery. The Sa Huynh people were highly skilled at making beads from glass, agate and precious stones. In particular, earrings with two animal heads and earrings with three pointed projections are the most characteristic artefacts. Similar jewellery has also been found in Thailand, the Philippines and other parts of the region. This shows that, from very early on, the Sa Huynh people had trade and exchange relations with coastal communities across Southeast Asia.

Alongside the jewellery are iron tools such as axes, knives and spades, as well as weapons, which reveal a considerable level of metalworking skill.

These discoveries help us understand that Hoi An's tradition of trade did not simply begin with the arrival of Japanese or Chinese merchant ships. Thousands of years earlier, the mouth of the Thu Bon River was already a place where people settled, made a living and connected with the outside world. After the Sa Huynh people came the Champa kingdom, with its trading port known as Lam Ap Pho, and later the port town of Hoi An that you are exploring today.

During your visit, please do not touch the artefacts and avoid using flash when taking photographs. We wish you a fascinating journey into the distant past.

title: Tan Ky Old House
summary: The first old house in Hoi An to be listed as a national heritage site, famous for its wood carvings and mother-of-pearl inlay.
content:
Welcome to Tan Ky Old House on Nguyen Thai Hoc Street. This is one of the most representative old houses in Hoi An, and it was the first old house here to be recognised as a National Historical and Cultural Relic, in 1985.

The house was built more than two hundred years ago and has been passed down through many generations of the same family. The name Tan Ky was given by the second generation of owners, expressing the hope that their business would always advance and prosper. The original owners were merchants who traded in goods such as silk, tea, precious timber, fish sauce and many local products.

Notice the layout of the house. It is a so-called tube house, narrow at the front and very deep, a style common in Hoi An. The front faces the street for trading, while the back opens towards the river, making it easy to unload goods from boats. In the middle is a small open-air courtyard that lets in light and breeze, cooling the whole house, and it is also a place for potted plants and a water basin that create a sense of calm.

The architecture of Tan Ky Old House blends three styles. The roof and the framework, with its stacked rafters, bear a Japanese imprint. The carvings, parallel sentences and decorative motifs are Chinese in style. And the arrangement of space and the familiar details are deeply Vietnamese. On the ceiling you can see carvings of crossed sabres wrapped in silk, symbolising strength and gentleness, along with peaches and bamboo, representing abundance and integrity.

What delights visitors most are the parallel sentences inlaid with mother-of-pearl hanging on the columns. If you look closely, you will see that each stroke of the Chinese characters is formed by the image of a bird in flight. This is an elaborate and unique decorative technique, revealing the refinement of the old artisans and the taste of the owners.

The house has also witnessed many great floods. On the wall, the water levels of historic flood years are marked, and on one occasion the water rose almost to the ceiling of the ground floor. Like many houses in Hoi An, Tan Ky has an upper floor with trapdoors, through which goods were lifted to safety when the water came.

Today, descendants of the family still live in and care for the house. During your visit, please walk softly, speak quietly and respect the owners' space. We hope you enjoy your time here.

title: Quan Thang Old House
summary: The wooden house of a Chinese family, notable for the carving art of the Kim Bong carpenters.
content:
Welcome to Quan Thang Old House on Tran Phu Street. Compared with some more famous houses, Quan Thang may be mentioned less often, yet it is an ideal place to fully appreciate the refined beauty and the living space of a merchant family in old Hoi An.

According to the family and local records, the house is about one hundred and fifty years old and belongs to a Chinese family that has lived in Hoi An for many generations.

The house follows the familiar tube house layout, consisting of a front house, an open courtyard, a connecting section and a rear house. The front room was used for trading and receiving guests. The open courtyard in the middle not only brings in light, air and rainwater, but is also a place to relax. Here you can see walls decorated with landscape paintings and potted ornamental plants, creating a feeling of tranquillity in the middle of the busy town.

The greatest highlight of Quan Thang Old House is its wood carving. The roof trusses, crossbeams, doors and balustrades are elaborately carved with dragons, phoenixes, flowers, birds and auspicious symbols. Most of these works are believed to have been made by artisans from the Kim Bong carpentry village. Kim Bong village lies on the other side of the Thu Bon River and has a history of several hundred years. Its craftsmen helped create the beauty of almost every wooden building in Hoi An Ancient Town.

Take a close look at how the wooden pieces fit together. The carpenters of old hardly used any iron nails. Instead, they used mortise and tenon joints and wooden pegs to connect the components. As a result, the house is both sturdy and slightly flexible, and each part can be dismantled and replaced when restoration is needed. This is the secret that has allowed Hoi An's wooden houses to survive for centuries in a hot, humid climate with frequent floods.

In the central room stands the ancestral altar, solemnly arranged with horizontal lacquered boards, parallel sentences and bronze ritual objects. For the family, this is the place where memories and traditions are kept, linking the generations together.

Quan Thang Old House shows us that every house in Hoi An is a living museum, where art, history and everyday life blend together. The family still lives here, so please visit quietly, keep order and do not touch the ritual objects. Thank you, and enjoy the rest of your journey through the ancient town.

title: Museum of Trade Ceramics
summary: A museum of trade ceramics from many countries, illustrating Hoi An's role as an international port.
content:
Welcome to the Museum of Trade Ceramics, housed in a beautiful two-storey wooden building on Tran Phu Street. Here you will discover the story of the maritime ceramic route and the role Hoi An played in the international trade network many centuries ago.

First, let us talk about the building itself. This old wooden house was restored in the early 1990s with the support of Japanese experts, following traditional techniques. You can observe the wooden framework, the open courtyard, the gallery and the staircase leading to the upper floor. The building itself is a precious exhibit that helps us understand how residents of the old town lived.

So what are trade ceramics? They are ceramic products made for buying, selling and exchanging between countries. From around the ninth to the nineteenth century, ceramics were among the most important goods on the sea routes linking East Asia, Southeast Asia, South Asia and the Middle East. Located in a favourable position near the river mouth and the sea, Hoi An became a stopover for many merchant fleets.

In the museum, you will see ceramics from many places: Chinese ceramics, Japanese ceramics, Thai ceramics, ceramics from the Middle East and, of course, Vietnamese ceramics. Many of these artefacts were found in the ground of Hoi An itself and the surrounding area. This proves that the port was once a meeting point for a great many different cultures.

Of particular interest are the artefacts related to the shipwreck discovered in the waters off the Cham Islands, not far from Hoi An. The ship is believed to have sunk around the fifteenth century, carrying a large cargo of Chu Dau ceramics, a famous type of blue and white ware from Hai Duong in northern Vietnam. The excavation in the late 1990s recovered hundreds of thousands of objects, causing a great stir among archaeologists and showing that Vietnamese ceramics were once exported widely around the world.

Take your time to admire the plates, bowls and vases decorated with dragons, phoenixes, lotus flowers, fish and landscapes. Each piece carries the traces of a long sea voyage, passing through the hands of potters, merchants and sailors from many nations.

The Museum of Trade Ceramics helps us understand why Hoi An became so wealthy and culturally diverse. During your visit, please do not touch the artefacts, take care on the wooden stairs and keep the space quiet. We hope you enjoy your discoveries.

title: Tran Family Chapel
summary: A family ancestral chapel built in the early 19th century to worship the ancestors of the Tran clan.
content:
Welcome to the Tran Family Chapel on Le Loi Street. Unlike the busy merchant houses along the streets, this place has a quiet and solemn atmosphere, set in a spacious garden surrounded by greenery. This is the ancestral chapel of the Tran family, one of the long-established clans of Hoi An.

According to the family's records, the ancestors of the Tran clan originated in China and came to Hoi An to make a living around the seventeenth or eighteenth century, gradually integrating into the Vietnamese community. The chapel was built around 1802, initiated by a mandarin of the family as a place to worship the ancestors and to gather the descendants.

An ancestral chapel is a very important institution in Vietnamese culture. It is where members of the clan come together to remember their grandparents and ancestors on death anniversaries and at Lunar New Year. It is also where the family genealogy is kept, where filial piety is taught and where the generations are bound together.

Look at the front of the chapel. The building has three entrances. According to old customs, men entered through the left door and women through the right door, while the central door was opened only on great occasions such as Lunar New Year, when it was believed that the spirits of the ancestors returned to visit their descendants. This arrangement reflects the order and rituals of traditional family life.

The architecture of the chapel is a harmonious blend of Vietnamese, Chinese and Japanese styles. The yin and yang roof tiles, the finely carved frame of precious wood, and the horizontal boards and parallel sentences lacquered in red and gold create a solemn appearance. Behind the altar, following the family tradition, there are small boxes containing the biographies and relics of the ancestors. On each death anniversary, the corresponding box is opened so that the descendants can remember that ancestor together.

Around the chapel is a garden with ornamental plants, a water basin and quiet corners. According to feng shui, green space and water help to balance yin and yang, bringing peace and good fortune to the clan. You may want to sit for a few minutes, listen to the birds and feel a slower pace of life, very different from the streets outside.

The Tran Family Chapel reveals a profound aspect of Hoi An's culture: the moral principle of remembering one's roots. It is still a family place of worship, so please dress respectfully, keep quiet and do not touch the ritual objects. Thank you for listening.

title: Fujian Assembly Hall
summary: The largest assembly hall in Hoi An, built by the Fujian Chinese community and dedicated to Thien Hau, the Goddess of the Sea.
content:
Welcome to the Fujian Assembly Hall, the largest and most magnificent of the Chinese assembly halls in Hoi An. From the colourful triple gate alone, you can sense the prosperity and status of the Fujian Chinese community in this port town.

According to records, this site was originally a small pagoda built at the end of the seventeenth century. In the mid-eighteenth century, the Fujian community bought it, expanded it and turned it into an assembly hall. Through several restorations and additions, the hall gradually took on the scale you see today. The triple gate you have just walked through was built later, in the second half of the twentieth century.

The hall is dedicated to Thien Hau, the Holy Mother of Heaven, also known as Mazu, the goddess who protects seafarers. Chinese people believe that she watches over merchant ships, guiding them through storms to arrive safely. For traders who spent months at sea, Thien Hau was an extremely important spiritual support. Beside her stand two deities: Thien Ly Nhan, who can see a thousand miles away, and Thuan Phong Nhi, who can hear the wind from very far off. They tell her when ships are in danger.

In the main hall, look out for the model of an old sailing junk, recalling the sea voyages of the Fujian ancestors. In the rear hall, six founding ancestors are worshipped. They were loyal followers of the Ming dynasty who migrated to Hoi An and are known as the Six Families. There is also an altar to the God of Wealth and, notably, a shrine to the Twelve Midwives together with the Goddess Kim Hoa. Many couples come here to pray for children, and when their wishes come true, they often return to give thanks.

Throughout the hall, you will see spiral incense coils hanging from the ceiling. Each coil can burn continuously for many days, carrying the prayers for health, peace and good fortune of the person who offered it.

Every year, the hall holds major festivals, such as the Lantern Festival on the fifteenth day of the first lunar month and the Feast of Thien Hau on the twenty-third day of the third lunar month, attracting large numbers of local people and visitors.

The Fujian Assembly Hall preserves the memories of people far from their homeland and symbolises the bond between the Chinese community and the land of Hoi An. During your visit, please keep quiet, do not touch the statues and be careful near the burning incense coils. Enjoy your visit.

title: Quan Cong Temple
summary: A 17th-century temple dedicated to Guan Yu, affectionately called Chua Ong by local people.
content:
Welcome to Quan Cong Temple, which the people of Hoi An affectionately call Chua Ong. The temple stands on Tran Phu Street, opposite Hoi An Market, and is one of the oldest religious buildings in the ancient town.

According to records, the temple was built around the middle of the seventeenth century, with contributions from both the Chinese community and the Vietnamese of Chinese descent, known as the Minh Huong people. It was restored many times in the following centuries. In 1991, Quan Cong Temple was recognised as a National Historical and Cultural Relic.

The temple is dedicated to Quan Cong, or Guan Yu, the famous general of the Three Kingdoms period in China. In East Asian culture, Guan Yu is a symbol of loyalty, righteousness, trustworthiness and courage. For the merchants of Hoi An, his image was a reminder of honesty in business and faithfulness to friends and partners. For this reason, the temple was once an important spiritual centre of the port.

As you enter the main hall, you will see a large statue of Guan Yu with a red face, a long beard and a green robe, radiating dignity. His red face symbolises loyalty and integrity. On either side stand statues of Chau Thuong, his faithful general holding a broadsword, and Quan Binh, his adopted son, holding the official seal.

On both sides of the entrance, you will notice two large horse statues, almost life size. One is white and the other red, the latter believed to be Red Hare, the legendary war horse closely associated with Guan Yu. Local people often come here to pray for peace, good luck and success in their work.

Now look up at the roof and the ridge. The decorations in glazed ceramics, depicting dragons, phoenixes and flowers, are finely crafted. In the courtyard there is a small pond and ornamental plants, creating a serene atmosphere. You may also notice the image of the carp in the decorations, recalling the legend of the carp that turns into a dragon, a symbol of perseverance and success.

On major festivals, especially the celebration of Guan Yu in the sixth lunar month, the temple is brightly decorated, traditional rituals are performed, and many local people come to offer incense.

Behind Quan Cong Temple is Quan Am Pagoda, now used as a space for historical and cultural exhibitions, which you can visit if you have time. While inside the temple, please keep quiet, dress respectfully and do not touch the statues. Thank you for listening.

title: Hoi An Market
summary: The riverside market on the Hoai River, the best place to feel everyday life and taste Hoi An's signature dishes.
content:
Welcome to Hoi An Market, the bustling heart of everyday life in the ancient town. If the assembly halls and old houses tell you about history, this market lets you feel Hoi An as it lives and breathes today, with its own colours, sounds and flavours.

The market occupies a prime location where Tran Phu Street meets Bach Dang Street, right beside the Hoai River. Back in the days of the thriving port, this riverside area was where boats docked and goods were busily exchanged. The market has existed for many generations and has been rebuilt and repaired several times, yet it remains the main trading centre for local people.

If you come early in the morning, head towards the riverbank. This is when the fishing boats come in, bringing fresh fish, squid and shrimp from the Cua Dai sea and the Thu Bon River. The calls of the vendors, the bargaining and the laughter blend together into a lively scene. People from nearby villages also bring vegetables, fruit and local produce to sell. Herbs from Tra Que, a famous vegetable village near Hoi An, are essential in many local dishes.

Inside the market is a food area where you can try the most typical dishes of Hoi An. First of all is cao lau, a noodle dish with chewy, golden brown noodles, served with sliced pork, fresh herbs and crispy rice crackers. Traditionally, cao lau noodles are made with water from the Ba Le well and wood ash, giving them a flavour found nowhere else. Next is mi Quang, the signature noodle dish of Quang Nam with its rich broth. There is also chicken rice, crispy pancakes called banh xeo, sweet soups and the famous Hoi An banh mi.

The fabric and tailoring section is another favourite with visitors. Hoi An is famous for tailors who can make an ao dai or a suit in a very short time. You can choose your fabric, have your measurements taken and collect the finished garment after one or two days.

When shopping at the market, it is a good idea to ask the price before buying and to bargain gently and politely. Keep an eye on your belongings in crowded places, and walk carefully, as the paths can be slippery and wet.

Hoi An Market is a place where you can chat with local people, enjoy authentic flavours and better understand the daily life of the ancient town's residents. We wish you a delicious and interesting experience.

title: Hainan Assembly Hall
summary: The assembly hall of the Hainan Chinese community, commemorating 108 merchants who were killed in the 19th century.
content:
Welcome to the Hainan Assembly Hall, located at the eastern end of Tran Phu Street. Compared with the other assembly halls in the ancient town, the Hainan Assembly Hall carries a special and moving story, linked to a tragic event in history.

The hall is the meeting place of the Chinese community from Hainan Island in China. According to records, it was built around 1875, during the reign of Emperor Tu Duc. However, the story of this place begins about twenty years earlier.

It is said that around 1851, one hundred and eight Hainanese merchants on their trading boats were killed by a naval commander, who then falsely accused them of being pirates in order to seize their property. Later, the truth came to light. Emperor Tu Duc had the commander punished, cleared the names of the victims and honoured them as heroic spirits, allowing a place of worship to be built for them. For this reason, the hall is also known as Chieu Ung Tu, the Temple of Response.

This means the hall is not only a meeting place for people from the same homeland, but also a memorial temple. As you enter the main hall, you will see a solemn altar dedicated to the one hundred and eight spirits. The atmosphere here is therefore more contemplative and profound than in the other assembly halls.

Take some time to admire the wood carving. The altar and the horizontal boards are extremely intricately carved and covered in glittering red lacquer and gold leaf. Dragons, phoenixes, flowers, scenes of daily life and stories from ancient tales are vividly portrayed, and they are considered among the finest wood carvings in the ancient town. The large columns, the roof trusses and the parallel sentences also display the refined skills of the craftsmen of old.

The layout of the hall follows traditional Chinese design, with a gate, a courtyard, a main hall and side rooms. Besides the main altar, the hall also worships Thien Hau, the Holy Mother who protects seafarers, a goddess very familiar to people who lived by the sea like the Hainanese.

The story of the Hainan Assembly Hall reminds us of the value of justice and of gratitude towards those who have passed away. It is also evidence of the long-standing bond between the Chinese community and the land of Hoi An. During your visit, please keep the space quiet, show respect and do not touch the ritual objects. Thank you for listening.

title: Chaozhou Assembly Hall
summary: The assembly hall of the Chaozhou Chinese community, renowned for some of the finest wood carving and porcelain mosaic in Hoi An.
content:
Welcome to the Chaozhou Assembly Hall on Nguyen Duy Hieu Street, on the eastern side of the ancient town. If you love decorative art, this is a stop you must not miss, because the Chaozhou Assembly Hall is considered to have the most exquisite carving in Hoi An.

The hall was built around 1845 by the Chinese community from Chaozhou, in Guangdong Province, China. The Chaozhou people were famous as skilful merchants and talented craftsmen. When they came to Hoi An, they founded this hall as a place for worship, for meetings and for supporting fellow countrymen.

The hall is dedicated to General Phuc Ba, or Ma Yuan, a general of the Han dynasty. In the beliefs of coastal Chinese communities, he was honoured as a god able to calm the waves and protect boats travelling at sea. For merchants who regularly crossed the ocean, this was a very important belief. In Vietnamese history, Ma Yuan was the commander of the Han army that suppressed the uprising of the Trung Sisters. His worship here therefore reflects the particular beliefs of the Chinese community, and it is also an interesting example of the cultural diversity of Hoi An.

Now let us admire the works of art. On the altar, the columns, the beams and the doors, the wood carvings depict dragons, phoenixes, flowers, birds, sea creatures and scenes from ancient legends. Every detail is carved in several layers, with real depth, as lifelike as can be. On the main doors, look for the two young women in traditional costume, carved with great softness and grace.

Besides wood, the Chaozhou Assembly Hall is also remarkable for its porcelain mosaic. On the roof and the walls, pieces of colourful ceramics are assembled into dragons, flowers and sacred animals. Their lines remain bright even after nearly two centuries of sun and rain.

The hall is not very large, but it is beautifully balanced, with a gate, an inner courtyard, a main hall and side rooms. Because it lies a little away from the centre, it is usually quieter, allowing you to take your time and observe every artistic detail.

The Chaozhou Assembly Hall is a testament to the talent of traditional craftsmen and to the richness of spiritual life in Hoi An. During your visit, please keep quiet and do not touch the carvings or the ritual objects. We wish you a truly rewarding visit.

title: Hoi An Museum
summary: A museum presenting the full history of Hoi An, from prehistory and Champa to the flourishing trading port.
content:
Welcome to the Hoi An Museum, where you can gain a complete picture of the history of this land. If you have already visited several individual sites in the ancient town, the museum will help you connect all those stories along a single timeline.

The story of Hoi An begins very early. The first exhibition area usually introduces the prehistoric and protohistoric periods, with traces of the Sa Huynh culture from more than two thousand years ago. Burial jars, jewellery made of precious stones and glass, and iron tools show that the ancient inhabitants here had a developed way of life and wide exchanges with surrounding regions.

Next comes the period of the Champa kingdom. For many centuries, the mouth of the Thu Bon River was an important trading port of the Cham people, often known as Lam Ap Pho. Not far from Hoi An lie the My Son sanctuary and the ancient capital of Tra Kieu, the religious and political centres of this kingdom. Cham statues, reliefs and ancient wells show cultural traces that are still present in the region.

From the fifteenth century onwards, this land gradually became part of Dai Viet. In the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, under the Nguyen lords, Hoi An flourished into an international trading port, which Western traders called Faifo. Merchants from Japan, China, Portugal, the Netherlands and many other countries came here to trade. The museum displays objects such as ceramics, ancient coins, maps and documents about the lively commercial activity of that time.

In the nineteenth century, when the river mouth silted up and large ships moved to the port of Da Nang, Hoi An gradually lost its role as a trading port. However, this is exactly what allowed the old town to escape the changes of urbanisation and to preserve its original appearance almost intact. In 1999, Hoi An Ancient Town was recognised by UNESCO as a World Cultural Heritage Site, as an exceptionally well-preserved example of a traditional trading port in Southeast Asia.

The museum also presents the struggles to defend the homeland and the cultural life of the people of Hoi An through the ages, from crafts such as Thanh Ha pottery and Kim Bong carpentry to traditional festivals.

Visiting the Hoi An Museum will help you understand more deeply why the ancient town is so exceptionally valuable. Please do not touch the exhibits, keep the space quiet and follow the instructions of the museum staff. We wish you a rewarding visit.

title: An Hoi Night Market and Lantern Street
summary: The night market by the Hoai River, glowing with thousands of lanterns, where you can release floating lanterns.
content:
Welcome to the An Hoi night market, on the bank of the Hoai River. As night falls, this becomes one of the most magical and romantic scenes in Hoi An, with thousands of colourful lanterns glowing and shimmering on the surface of the water.

An Hoi is an islet on the southern bank of the Hoai River, connected to the ancient town by the An Hoi Bridge. The night market stretches along Nguyen Hoang Street, with many stalls selling lanterns, souvenirs, clothes, handicrafts and tempting street food.

Lanterns have become a symbol of Hoi An. Lantern making here is believed to date back to the days of the trading port, when Chinese merchants hung lanterns in front of their houses to bring luck and peace. Over time, the Vietnamese adopted and developed the craft, creating lanterns with a style unique to Hoi An. A traditional lantern is made from a flexible bamboo frame covered with colourful silk. The craftsman must skilfully split the bamboo, bend the frame, stretch the fabric and glue every edge. Many lanterns can be folded flat, making them very convenient for visitors to take home as gifts.

One experience you should not miss here is releasing a floating lantern on the Hoai River. You can take a small boat along the river or stand on the bank, light a candle inside a small paper lantern shaped like a lotus flower and gently place it on the water. According to folk belief, each lantern carries a wish for the health, happiness and good fortune of yourself and your loved ones.

If you are lucky enough to be in Hoi An on the fourteenth day of the lunar month, you can join the Ancient Town Night. On that evening, many households in the old quarter turn off their electric lights and light the streets only with lanterns. Traditional cultural activities take place, such as bai choi folk singing, Chinese chess and performances on traditional musical instruments, creating a very special, nostalgic atmosphere.

At the night market, you can also enjoy snacks such as grilled rice paper, crispy pancakes, grilled skewers, sweet soups and refreshing cold drinks. When shopping, ask the price first and bargain cheerfully and politely.

This area is very crowded in the evening, so keep a careful eye on your belongings and take care when walking near the riverbank or getting on and off boats. Please help keep the river clean by not throwing rubbish into the water. We wish you an unforgettable evening under the lanterns of Hoi An.
